listen_text: Chapter. Intuitionistic Tableaux. Editorial note. Draft chapter on prefixed tableaux for intuitionistic logic. Needs more examples, completeness proofs, and discussion of how one can find countermodels from unsuccessful searches for closed tableaux. End editorial note.

Section. Introduction. Tableaux are certain (downward-branching) trees of signed formulas, that is, pairs consisting of a truth value sign ( true or false ) and a sentence Displayed expression. signed true A, or signed false A. End displayed expression. A tableau begins with a number of assumptions. Each further signed formula is generated by applying one of the inference rules. Some inference rules add one or more signed formulas to a tip of the tree; others add two new tips, resulting in two branches. Rules result in signed formulas where the formula is less complex than that of the signed formula to which it was applied. When a branch contains both signed true A and signed false A , we say the branch is closed. If every branch in a tableau is closed, the entire tableau is closed. A closed tableau constitutes a derivation that shows that the set of signed formulas which were used to begin the tableau are unsatisfiable. This can be used to define a proves relation: Gamma proves A if and only if there is some finite set Gamma sub zero equals the finite set containing B sub one through B sub n, and is a subset of Gamma such that there is a closed tableau for the assumptions Displayed expression. the set containing signed false A and signed true B sub one through signed true B sub n. End displayed expression. For intuitionistic logic, we have to both extend the notion of signed formula and adjust the rules for the connectives. In addition to a sign( true or false ), formulas in modal tableaux also have prefixes sigma . The prefixes are non-empty sequences of positive integers, that is, sigma is a nonempty finite sequence of positive integers . When we write such prefixes without the surrounding angle-bracket sequence notation , and separate the individual elements by a dot apostrophe s instead of a comma apostrophe s . If sigma is a prefix, then prefix sigma dot n is prefix sigma concatenated with the one-element sequence n ; for example, if sigma equals prefix one dot two dot one , then prefix sigma dot three is prefix one dot two dot one dot three . So for instance, Displayed expression. signed true, if A then if B then C, at prefix one dot two. End displayed expression. is a prefixed signed formula (or just a prefixed formula for short). Intuitively, the prefix names a world in a model that might satisfy the formulas on a branch of a tableau, and if sigma names some world, then prefix sigma dot n names a world accessible from (the world named by) sigma . In intuitionistic models, the accessibility relation is reflexive and transitive. In terms of prefixes, this means that sigma is accessible from sigma itself, and so is any prefix that extends sigma , that is, any prefix of the form prefix sigma dot n sub one, continuing through dot n sub k . Let's introduce the notation prefix sigma dot star to indicate sigma itself and any extension of it. In other words, the prefixes prefix sigma dot star are all and only the prefixes accessible from sigma . End section.

listen_text: Section. Rules for Intuitionistic Logic. The rules for the connectives conjunction and disjunction are the same as for regular propositional signed tableaux, just with prefixes added. In each case, the rule applied to a signed formula signed A with sign S at prefix sigma produces new formulas that are also prefixed by sigma . This should be intuitively clear: for example, if A and B is true at (a world named by) sigma , then A and B are true at sigma (and not at any other world). We collect the rules for conjunction and disjunction in the prefixed conjunction and disjunction rule table . Displayed expression. Four prefixed propositional tableau rules, read across each source row. Row one left, signed true A and B at sigma yields signed true A and then signed true B at sigma. Row one right, signed false A and B at sigma branches to signed false A or signed false B at sigma. Row two left, signed true A or B at sigma branches to signed true A or signed true B at sigma. Row two right, signed false A or B at sigma yields signed false A and then signed false B at sigma. End of rule table. End displayed expression. Caption connective labels, in source order: conjunction , then disjunction . End of table. The closure condition is similar to that for ordinary tableaux, although we require that not just the formulas, but also that the prefixes must match. In fact, we can be somewhat more liberal: Since in intuitionistic models, formulas, once true, remain true, it is impossible that A is true at sigma but false at any accessible prefix prefix sigma dot star . So a branch is closed if it contains both Displayed expression. signed true A at prefix sigma, and signed false A at an accessible prefix sigma dot star. End displayed expression. for some prefix sigma and formula A . Note that if the signs are reversed, that is, if it contains Displayed expression. signed false A at prefix sigma, and signed true A at an accessible prefix sigma dot star. End displayed expression. the branch is closed only if star is the empty sequence. In addition, a branch is closed if it contains signed true falsity at prefix sigma . The rules for setting up assumptions is also as for ordinary tableaux, except that for assumptions we always use the prefix one . (It does not matter which prefix we use, as long as it's the same for all assumptions.) So, for example, we say that Displayed expression. B sub one through B sub n prove A. End displayed expression. if and only if there is a closed tableau for the assumptions Displayed expression. signed true B sub one through signed true B sub n at prefix one, followed by signed false A at prefix one. End displayed expression. For the conditional conditional , the rules differ from the classical and modal cases. The the signed-true conditional rule extends a branch containing signed true, if A then B, at prefix sigma by signed true A at prefix sigma dot star and signed false B at prefix sigma dot star on two different branches. It can only be applied for a prefix prefix sigma dot star which already occurs on the branch in which it is applied. Let's call such a prefix “used” (on the branch). (Since prefix sigma dot star includes sigma itself, the rule can always be applied by adding the prefixed signed formulas signed true A at prefix sigma and signed false B at prefix sigma on separate branches.) The the signed-false conditional rule extends a branch containing signed false, if A then B, at prefix sigma by both signed true A at prefix sigma dot n and signed false B at prefix sigma dot n on the same branch, with prefix sigma dot n a prefix new to the branch. The rules for negation are defined analogously (using the definition of not A as if A then falsity ). The rules are given in the prefixed negation and conditional rule table . Displayed expression. Four prefixed tableau rules, read across each source row. Row one left, signed true not A at sigma yields signed false A at used accessible prefix sigma dot star. Row one right, signed false not A at sigma yields signed true A at a new prefix sigma dot n. Row two left, signed true if A then B at sigma branches to signed false A or signed true B at a used accessible prefix sigma dot star. Row two right, signed false if A then B at sigma yields signed true A and then signed false B at a new prefix sigma dot n. End of rule table. End displayed expression. Caption connective labels, in source order: negation , then conditional . End of table. End section.

By the signed-false conditional rule on node two: signed true A at prefix one dot one , then signed false, if B then C, at prefix one dot one . By the signed-false conditional rule on node four: signed true B at prefix one dot one dot one , then signed false C at prefix one dot one dot one . The signed-true conditional rule on node one splits from node six. listen_text: Section. Soundness for Intuitionistic Tableaux. In order to show that intuitionistic tableaux are sound, we have to show that if Displayed expression. signed true B sub one through signed true B sub n at prefix one, followed by signed false A at prefix one. End displayed expression. has a closed tableau then B sub one through B sub n entail A . It is easier to prove the contrapositive: if for some model capital M and world w , in model capital M at world w, B sub i is satisfied for all i equals one , and so on, n but in model capital M at world w, A is satisfied , then no tableau can close. Such a countermodel shows that the initial assumptions of the tableau are satisfiable. The strategy of the proof is to show that whenever all the prefixed formulas on a tableau branch are satisfiable, any application of a rule results in at least one extended branch that is also satisfiable. Since closed branches are unsatisfiable, any tableau for a satisfiable set of prefixed formulas must have at least one open branch. Source anomaly note. Source proof caveat. The stated contrapositive calls this a countermodel, so its last satisfaction sign should be negative, but the source prints that A is satisfied. The original formula is retained. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. In order to apply this strategy in the modal case, we have to extend our definition of “satisfiable” to relational and prefixes. With that in hand, however, the proof is straightforward. Definition. Let P be some set of prefixes, that is, P is a subset of the nonempty finite sequences of positive integers and let model capital M be a model. A function f is a function from the prefix set P to the world set W is an interpretation of P in model capital M if, whenever sigma and prefix sigma dot n are both in P , then f of sigma bears R to f of sigma dot n . Relative to an interpretation of prefixes P we can define: List. Next item. model capital M satisfies signed true A at prefix sigma if and only if in model capital M at the world f of sigma, A is satisfied . Next item. model capital M satisfies signed false A at prefix sigma if and only if in model capital M at the world f of sigma, A is not satisfied . End list. End definition. Note that since R is reflexive and transitive and prefix sigma dot star denotes, sigma , prefix sigma dot n sub one , prefix sigma dot n sub one dot n sub two , and so on, we also have that f of sigma bears R to f of prefix sigma dot star . Definition. Let Gamma be a set of prefixed formulas, and let P of Gamma, the set of prefixes occurring in Gamma be the set of prefixes that occur in it. If f is an interpretation of P of Gamma, the set of prefixes occurring in Gamma in model capital M , we say that model capital M satisfies Gamma with respect to f , model capital M satisfies Gamma with respect to f , if model capital M satisfies every prefixed formula in Gamma with respect to f . Gamma is satisfiable if and only if there is a model model capital M and interpretation f of P of Gamma, the set of prefixes occurring in Gamma such that model capital M satisfies Gamma with respect to f . End definition. Proposition. If Gamma contains both signed true A at prefix sigma and signed false A at prefix sigma dot star for some formula A and prefix sigma , or it contains signed true falsity at prefix sigma , then Gamma is unsatisfiable. End proposition. Proof. Since always in model capital M at the world f of sigma, falsity is not satisfied , a Gamma that contains signed true falsity is unsatisfiable. There also cannot be a model model capital M and interpretation f of P of Gamma, the set of prefixes occurring in Gamma such that both If in model capital M at the world f of sigma, A is satisfied , then by the earlier proposition that intuitionistic truth persists along accessibility , since f of sigma bears R to prefix sigma dot star , in model capital M at the world f of sigma, A is satisfied . So we cannot have both in model capital M at the world f of sigma, A is satisfied and in model capital M at the world f of sigma dot star, A is not satisfied . End proof. Source anomaly note. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. Theorem. Soundness. If Gamma has a closed tableau, Gamma is unsatisfiable. End theorem. Proof. We call a branch of a tableau satisfiable if and only if the set of signed formulas on it is satisfiable, and let's call a tableau satisfiable if it contains at least one satisfiable branch. We show the following: Extending a satisfiable tableau by one of the rules of inference always results in a satisfiable tableau. This will prove the theorem: any closed tableau results by applying rules of inference to the tableau consisting only of assumptions from Gamma . So if Gamma were satisfiable, any tableau for it would be satisfiable. A closed tableau, however, is clearly not satisfiable, since all its branches are closed and closed branches are unsatisfiable. Suppose we have a satisfiable tableau, that is, a tableau with at least one satisfiable branch. Applying a rule of inference either adds signed formulas to a branch, or splits a branch in two. If the tableau has a satisfiable branch which is not extended by the rule application in question, it remains a satisfiable branch in the extended tableau, so the extended tableau is satisfiable. So we only have to consider the case where a rule is applied to a satisfiable branch. Let Gamma be the set of signed formulas on that branch, and let signed A with sign S at prefix sigma is a member of Gamma be the signed formula to which the rule is applied. If the rule does not result in a split branch, we have to show that the extended branch, that is, Gamma together with the conclusions of the rule, is still satisfiable. If the rule results in split branch, we have to show that at least one of the two resulting branches is satisfiable. List. Next item.
